title: In re World Trade Center Disaster Site Litigation
lead: Workers alleging toxic exposure during September 11 recovery faced emergency-immunity defenses from local and private participants. The appeal separated immunity from liability from immunity from suit, then recognized a possible derivative federal defense while finding collaboration alone insufficient for judgment.

actors.name: Rescue, recovery, and cleanup workers
actors.role: Plaintiffs alleging respiratory injury from toxic exposure

actors.name: New York City and its Department of Design and Construction
Contractors, Port Authority, and property owners
Judge Hellerstein
actors.role: District judge rejecting the asserted defenses

actors.name: Judge Wesley
actors.role: Author of the unanimous appellate opinion

proceedings: After denial of state immunity on the pleadings and federal immunity on summary judgment, defendants sought collateral-order review. The Second Circuit dismissed the state portion and affirmed denial of federal summary judgment on March 26, 2008.
limits: The mixed mandate left suits pending and decided no negligence, causation, damages, later settlement, or special-master issue. Possible derivative immunity remained available on an adequately developed record, and specified statutory and jurisdictional issues were reserved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Recovery workers alleged failures of protection and warning
sections.cue: Introduce the underlying claims and federal setting.
paragraphs: Workers performing rescue, recovery, and cleanup after September 11 alleged respiratory injuries from toxic exposure. They accused New York City and its Department of Design and Construction, contractors, the Port Authority, and World Trade Center property owners of failing to monitor conditions, provide protection, and warn. Negligence and New York labor and municipal statutes supplied the asserted duties. No breach or causal injury had been established in the appeal.

The Air Transportation Safety and System Stabilization Act brought the litigation into federal court. Earlier rulings addressed which recovery activities fell within its exclusive federal cause and jurisdiction; its substantive-law provision generally borrowed state law unless inconsistent with or preempted by federal law. The present appeal did not redetermine every claim’s federal character.

sections.title: Defendants sought immediate review of immunity denials
sections.cue: Trace the ruling and the claimed federal direction.
paragraphs: District Judge Hellerstein rejected state-law immunity on the pleadings and federal immunity on summary judgment. Defendants described federally coordinated disaster response, including the Army Corps’ Fresh Kills work, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s respiratory-protection role, and Environmental Protection Agency activities. They argued that litigation threatened emergency discretion. Workers disputed federal direction of the particular allegedly negligent acts.

The district court declined interlocutory certification under section 1292(b), so defendants invoked the collateral-order doctrine. An earlier appellate ruling had lifted a stay and restored trial-level proceedings. Judge Wesley’s opinion, joined by Judges Newman and Sotomayor, now considered immediate appealability and the asserted derivative federal protection.

sections.title: State protections against liability did not authorize this appeal
sections.cue: Explain the distinction governing collateral review.
paragraphs: A collateral order must conclusively decide an important issue separate from merits and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Litigation expense alone was insufficient. Immunity from suit could be lost by undergoing suit; a liability defense survived for final review. Calling a defense immunity did not decide its nature. Legal entitlement could be reviewed on the workers’ accepted facts, not through resolving contested conduct.

State law defined the state protections, while federal law controlled finality. New York’s permissive appeal practices did not automatically create a federal collateral order. The State Defense Emergency Act and Disaster Act protected qualifying actors from liability; other statutes expressly barred both liability and action. That distinction and Brown, the state precedent construing governmental immunity, showed protection from liability rather than litigation itself. Emergency-policy concerns could not enlarge it.

The Port Authority’s broad statutory consent to suit and interstate-agency precedents also defeated general sovereign immunity from suit. A residual governmental-function defense remained possible but could not support this immediate appeal. The court dismissed the state portion for lack of appellate jurisdiction rather than affirming its substantive rejection.

sections.title: Federal disaster immunity could extend derivatively in a proper case
sections.cue: Explain the threshold and adapted contractor test.
paragraphs: Stafford Act section 305, 42 U.S.C. section 5148, protected the federal government’s discretionary disaster-assistance functions. Despite wording resembling state provisions, federal sovereign-immunity history, legislative background, and separation of powers made it immunity from suit. That construction did not override New York’s treatment of its own laws.

These defendants were not federal agencies or employees. Drawing on Yearsley and Boyle, precedents addressing protection for conduct implementing federal authority, the court recognized derivative protection when state liability significantly conflicted with a protected federal decision. Any categorical district-court rejection of that possibility was erroneous, but did not entitle defendants to judgment.

First, a federal agency itself had to qualify: action within the Stafford Act, permissible judgment rather than breach of a mandatory rule, and public-policy discretion rather than every practical choice. The parties had inadequately briefed that threshold, requiring initial district-court consideration.

The adapted Boyle inquiry then required reasonably precise federally approved specifications, federal supervision and control of implementation, and disclosure of dangers known to the implementer but not the agency. Substantive approval mattered. Meetings, cooperation, or a rubber stamp did not establish implementation of a protected federal decision.

sections.title: General collaboration did not prove protection for the challenged acts
sections.cue: Apply the framework without deciding disputed facts.
paragraphs: For example, implementing a sufficiently precise protected federal respiratory policy under supervision with required warnings might qualify. A locally chosen policy receiving nominal federal approval would not, nor would failure to follow actual federal requirements. These were illustrations, not factual conclusions.

The evidence showed collaboration but did not sufficiently distinguish federal directions from independent choices. The court therefore affirmed denial of federal summary judgment while preserving a possible later defense on proper support. It did not settle disputed evidentiary questions through collateral review.

The Port Authority’s reliance on Pani and Murray, cases concerning particular governmental functions or delegations, did not transfer sovereign immunity to every government assistant. No equivalent compulsory delegation of the challenged conduct was demonstrated. Property ownership and vicarious-liability claims did not become governmental acts merely through recovery participation. A disaster-payment regulation likewise did not make the United States the real party in interest in all recipient suits: funding was conditional and excluded recipients’ negligence expenses.

sections.title: Emergency policy concerns did not justify blanket immunity
sections.cue: State the mandate and remaining reservations.
paragraphs: The court acknowledged concern about discouraging future responders but left broader protection to Congress; contractors could manage risk through compensation, insurance, and indemnification. Emergency declarations did not simply suspend labor laws, though genuinely conflicting requirements could displace them.

The court reserved whether Stafford immunity covered abuse of discretion, constitutional issues concerning possible new legislation, and appellate jurisdiction over the contention that the aviation statute preempted immunity defenses. It denied dismissal of the federal-immunity appeal, affirmed denial of federal summary judgment, and dismissed the state appeal: dismissed in part and affirmed in part. An amicus could file a brief but received no further participation.
The unanimous March 26, 2008 judgment left the workers’ suits pending. It did not decide the later settlement, the separate September 11 compensation fund, or a Rule 53 special-master question.
